A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, and their main text and appendices can be matched reliably. However, v2 Figure 13 lacks readable numerical axis, color-scale and legend labels, limiting quantitative interpretation of that added analysis. The remaining material supports comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations evaluating drift recovery on four stochastic systems, including benchmark comparisons, noise sensitivity and metric-learning ablations in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds higher-dimensional simulations, geometric-weight sensitivity, convergence experiments and comparisons with Onsager–Machlup paths.

M1.justification: The learned metric, geodesic construction, controlled bridge augmentation and Gaussian-process drift updates remain the same. Algorithms A1–A3 are retained. Expanded explanations of soft geometric constraints and corrections to equations do not establish a changed inference procedure.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates four two-dimensional systems. v2 adds a three-dimensional Repressilator and Van der Pol dynamics embedded in five- and eight-dimensional stochastic environments, with additional noise and restoring forces outside the embedded subspace. Appendix G also examines embedded systems across dimensions 3–10. These extend the represented dynamics and observation environments.

E2.justification: Appendix I.6 adds straight-line interpolation as a comparator for learned geodesics, using numerically computed ground-truth Onsager–Machlup minimizers as reference. Existing drift-estimation comparators remain; the RBF comparisons move to Table 3. WLF-AM disappears from J.2's list, but v1 contains no identifiable corresponding result, so a evaluated-baseline removal is not established.

E3.justification: Retained benchmark settings remain unchanged, but v2 introduces substantial additional evaluation designs: beta sweeps over 0.1, 0.5, 1 and 2; augmentation beyond two iterations with negative-log-likelihood tracking; covariance participation-ratio measurements; and Onsager–Machlup comparisons using path distance and action gaps across sampling intervals, trajectory lengths, metric bandwidths and noise levels.

E4.justification: v2 adds geometric-weight sensitivity in Figure 6, effective-dimensionality analysis in Figure 7, convergence analysis in Figure 12, and direct examination of the geodesic approximation in Figures 13–14. These investigate robustness, optimization and the method's geometric premise. Existing noise-misestimation and metric-learning ablations are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Existing mean-and-standard-deviation reporting is retained. New analyses introduce different replication and reporting details: Figure 6 reports three-run averages, Figure 12 specifies five versus three runs, and Appendix I.6 specifies three independent runs with 20 observation intervals per run. These additions do not establish increased replication of the original benchmarks.

E6.justification: Matched benchmark values are retained, including Table 1's Geometric wRMSE of 0.750 ± 0.038 at sigma = 0.50 and tau = 240 dt; relocated metric-ablation values also match. v2 adds substantial numerical and qualitative findings on higher-dimensional recovery, beta sensitivity, effective dimensionality, convergence and geodesic approximation. These are additional results, rather than improved scores for the original comparisons.

T1.justification: Appendix H.2.1 revises repeated-integral weights from (t-u) to (t-u)^2/2 and changes the stated curvature-remainder and drift-bias orders from O(tau^2)/O(tau) to O(tau^3)/O(tau^2). Appendix K adds componentwise time and memory complexity analysis. The mathematical revision remains incomplete: v2 Eqs. 92–93 retain approximations proportional to tau^2/2 and tau/2 despite the revised integrals and stated orders.

C1.justification: The abstract's principal claim of geometry-guided recovery from sparse observations is retained. However, v1 Sections 3 and 5 identify learned geodesics with most-probable paths, whereas v2 describes them as geometry-informed reference curves and acknowledges that they generally differ from Onsager–Machlup minimizers. This narrows a supporting scientific claim.

C2.justification: v2 substantially clarifies the method's interpretation: sparse observations can admit multiple drift hypotheses, and the geometric penalty favors hypotheses whose paths follow high-density regions. It explains geodesics as approximate soft constraints, motivates two iterations as a computational tradeoff, and newly acknowledges synthetic-only validation and an implementation not optimized for high-dimensional scalability.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit code-repository availability statement, Repressilator equations and simulation settings, and detailed discrete Onsager–Machlup optimization using three nested temporal grids. Appendix K documents storage of augmented trajectories and computational requirements. These substantially expand reproducibility information, while the original algorithms and retained experimental settings remain documented.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature such as Jacobs et al. (2023), Gao et al. (2024), Bae et al. (2025), and Zhang and Stumpf (2026), and expands discussion of multi-marginal and nonequilibrium Schrödinger bridges. The principal positioning against temporal inference and population-transport methods remains. Numerous other reference changes merely update publication metadata.

P1.justification: The introduction is refocused around sparse-sampling identifiability and gains an explicit contribution list. Background derivations are condensed, control explanations expanded, and the discussion reorganized under thematic headings. Literature and metric-learning discussion move into appendices, the Impact Statement moves before the references, and the LLM-usage statement is removed.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main text, restyles typography and captions, relocates figures, and regroups metric-ablation results into Table 3. It adds eight figures and a computational-cost table, while retained plots gain sampling-unit labels. Presentation defects include the repeated placeholder running title and missing numerical labels in Figure 13.

improvement.justification: v2 improves empirical support through previously absent beta-sensitivity, convergence and higher-dimensional checks, and more accurately qualifies the geodesic premise. Added implementation and code-access information also helps reproducibility. The net gain is limited by incomplete mathematical corrections in H.2.1, especially Eqs. 92–93, and missing Figure 13 labels that obstruct interpretation of an important new validation experiment.
